questions.question: What were Practice Administrators worried about at the Invite your team step?

questions.question: Which onboarding steps are required, and which can be skipped?

seeded.answer:
The Compass AI practice setup requires completion of every step; skipping is not possible in the current build [1][2]. Specifically, steps 3 (Connect calendar) and 4 (Invite your team) have no “Connect later” or “Skip for now” options [1].

The dashboard review of January 20, 2026, showed that 7 of 24 setups stalled at the Connect calendar step, and 3 at Invite your team [3]. The usability test on February 3, 2026, confirmed that 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at Connect calendar because they believed IT should approve access to the appointment schedule, and 3 hesitated at Invite your team due to concerns about emailing staff before training [4][5]. IT Administrator P160 confirmed that a privacy review request, filed by IT not a Practice Administrator, is required before a new system can read the practice’s appointment schedule [6].

sources.title: Compass AI Practice Setup — The Five Steps as Built
sources.excerpt:
Every step is required. "Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it" (2026-01-20 :34-35 ). For steps 3 and 4: "There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it" (2026-02-03 :36-37 ).
When a setup counts as started, and as stopped. "A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20" (2026-01-20 :35-36 ).

sources.title: Dashboard review — Compass AI practice setup completion
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the Compass AI practice setup flow, the flow a practice's administrator uses to set Compass AI up for their practice, to see where setups stop and how long they stay stopped. This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training. The dashboard records setups, not why a practice started one or which Compass AI features it was setting up for, and the corpus doesn't record how practices were chosen to set up or when each planned to go live. This review is not tied to the ambient scribe GA: the GA candidate was still under test on 2026-01-13 ( 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ).
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal usage dashboard for the practice setup flow, covering setups started 2025-12-01 to 2026-01-16 (seven weeks), with step status as of the review date, 2026-01-20
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Context: The flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, 5 Review & finish. Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it. A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20. The dashboard shows setups by practice; it doesn't show the signed-in person's role, so whether a Practice Administrator or an IT Administrator ran each setup isn't known. The number of practices in the network isn't on the dashboard and isn't recorded in the corpus, so no completion rate against all practices is given here.
Counts (24 setups started in the window):
Finished (completed Review & finish): 12 of 24
Still open on 2026-01-20: 12 of 24, stopped at:
Practice details: 1 of 24, open 5 days
Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)
Invite your team: 3 of 24, open 6, 11 and 19 days
Review & finish: 1 of 24, open 2 days
Reached Review & finish: 13 of 24 (the 12 finished plus the 1 still open there)
Key Findings
[HIGH] (stall at Connect calendar) Connect calendar is where setups stop most: 7 of the 24 setups started (7 of the 12 still open) were open at that step on 2026-01-20, and they had sat there longest, 4 to 41 days (median 16). In the 12 finished setups, Connect calendar was also the step left open longest in 8 of 12.
[MEDIUM] (stall at Invite your team) Invite your team is the second most common stopping point: 3 of 24 setups started (3 of the 12 still open), open 6, 11 and 19 days.
[LOW] (other steps) 1 of 24 was open at Practice details (5 days) and 1 of 24 at Review & finish (2 days). No setup was open at Sign in, because a setup only counts as started once someone has signed in.
Representative Quotes
None — this session has no participants.
Recommendations
Run a moderated usability test of the setup flow with both Practice Administrators and IT Administrators, focused on Connect calendar and Invite your team, to find out why setups stop there.
Ask the dashboard owners whether the signed-in person's role can be shown per setup, so later reviews can tell Practice Administrator setups from IT Administrator ones.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why do setups stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team? A dashboard can't show reasons: it records where a setup is open and for how long, not what the person at that step was thinking or waiting for.
Do stopped setups eventually finish, or are they abandoned? Re-check these 12 open setups at the next review.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.

sources.title: Dashboard review — Compass AI practice setup completion
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the Compass AI practice setup flow, the flow a practice's administrator uses to set Compass AI up for their practice, to see where setups stop and how long they stay stopped. The dashboard records setups, not why a practice started one or which Compass AI features it was setting up for, and the corpus doesn't record how practices were chosen to set up or when each planned to go live. Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal usage dashboard for the practice setup flow, covering setups started 2025-12-01 to 2026-01-16 (seven weeks), with step status as of the review date, 2026-01-20
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Context: The flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, 5 Review & finish. Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it. A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20. The dashboard shows setups by practice; it doesn't show the signed-in person's role, so whether a Practice Administrator or an IT Administrator ran each setup isn't known. The number of practices in the network isn't on the dashboard and isn't recorded in the corpus, so no completion rate against all practices is given here.
Counts (24 setups started in the window):
Finished (completed Review & finish): 12 of 24
Still open on 2026-01-20: 12 of 24, stopped at:
Practice details: 1 of 24, open 5 days
Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)
Invite your team: 3 of 24, open 6, 11 and 19 days
Review & finish: 1 of 24, open 2 days
Reached Review & finish: 13 of 24 (the 12 finished plus the 1 still open there)
Key Findings
[HIGH] (stall at Connect calendar) Connect calendar is where setups stop most: 7 of the 24 setups started (7 of the 12 still open) were open at that step on 2026-01-20, and they had sat there longest, 4 to 41 days (median 16). In the 12 finished setups, Connect calendar was also the step left open longest in 8 of 12.
[MEDIUM] (stall at Invite your team) Invite your team is the second most common stopping point: 3 of 24 setups started (3 of the 12 still open), open 6, 11 and 19 days.
[LOW] (other steps) 1 of 24 was open at Practice details (5 days) and 1 of 24 at Review & finish (2 days). No setup was open at Sign in, because a setup only counts as started once someone has signed in.
Representative Quotes
None — this session has no participants.
Recommendations
Run a moderated usability test of the setup flow with both Practice Administrators and IT Administrators, focused on Connect calendar and Invite your team, to find out why setups stop there.
Ask the dashboard owners whether the signed-in person's role can be shown per setup, so later reviews can tell Practice Administrator setups from IT Administrator ones.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why do setups stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team? A dashboard can't show reasons: it records where a setup is open and for how long, not what the person at that step was thinking or waiting for.
Do stopped setups eventually finish, or are they abandoned? Re-check these 12 open setups at the next review.

sources.title: Interview — IT Administrator on Schedule Access and Staff Invites
sources.excerpt:
Objective
In the 2026-02-03 usability test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at Connect calendar because they did not think they could approve Compass AI's access to patient appointments, and both IT Administrators asked which fields are read before connecting ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:51-52 ). This session asked one IT Administrator who approves access requests across practices what has to happen before a new system can read a practice's appointment schedule, and who can start that. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training (in 2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:62 , "onboarding" means training copy for clinicians).
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an IT Administrator who handles access requests for systems used across Meridian's practices. They had not used the Compass AI practice setup flow. The researcher described steps 3 (Connect calendar) and 4 (Invite your team) as the 2026-02-03 build shows them, and what the step 3 screen does and doesn't say, without sharing what other participants said. The participant did not name the scheduling system that holds the appointment schedule, and these notes don't record which system it is. This is their account of the approval process, not a review of its records.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (schedule access: privacy review) In their account, any new system that reads the appointment schedule needs a privacy review request before it is connected, and a Practice Administrator can't start one: requests are filed by IT. A practice that wants the calendar connected has to ask IT to file the request. They didn't know whether one had been filed for Compass AI.
[MEDIUM] (schedule access: still PHI) They described scheduling as the lowest-risk data on the CMIO's PHI ordering, but still PHI: the schedule carries patient names and, depending on the fields read, visit reasons. They saw this as consistent with the ordering, not a contradiction of it, because the ordering ranks the risk and doesn't remove the review.
Representative Quotes
"Lowest risk isn't no risk. It's still patient names on a schedule. It still goes through privacy review, it just shouldn't take long." — IT Administrator, P160
"A practice admin can't put in that request. They call us, we file it. If the screen just asks them to click connect, it's asking the wrong person." — IT Administrator, P160
Recommendations
On Connect calendar, route an administrator who can't approve schedule access to IT, consistent with the "Send to IT for approval" path recommended on 2026-02-03 ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:75-76 ).
Before more practices set up, confirm with IT whether a privacy review request for Compass AI reading the appointment schedule has been filed, and list the fields it covers.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Has a privacy review request for Compass AI's schedule access been filed, and which fields does it cover?
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through the setup flow's invites, or both? The participant didn't know.

sources.title: Dashboard review — Compass AI practice setup completion
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the Compass AI practice setup flow, the flow a practice's administrator uses to set Compass AI up for their practice, to see where setups stop and how long they stay stopped. This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training. The dashboard records setups, not why a practice started one or which Compass AI features it was setting up for, and the corpus doesn't record how practices were chosen to set up or when each planned to go live. This review is not tied to the ambient scribe GA: the GA candidate was still under test on 2026-01-13 ( 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ).
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal usage dashboard for the practice setup flow, covering setups started 2025-12-01 to 2026-01-16 (seven weeks), with step status as of the review date, 2026-01-20
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Context: The flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, 5 Review & finish. Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it. A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20. The dashboard shows setups by practice; it doesn't show the signed-in person's role, so whether a Practice Administrator or an IT Administrator ran each setup isn't known. The number of practices in the network isn't on the dashboard and isn't recorded in the corpus, so no completion rate against all practices is given here.
Counts (24 setups started in the window):
Finished (completed Review & finish): 12 of 24
Still open on 2026-01-20: 12 of 24, stopped at:
Practice details: 1 of 24, open 5 days
Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)
Invite your team: 3 of 24, open 6, 11 and 19 days
Review & finish: 1 of 24, open 2 days
Reached Review & finish: 13 of 24 (the 12 finished plus the 1 still open there)
Key Findings
[HIGH] (stall at Connect calendar) Connect calendar is where setups stop most: 7 of the 24 setups started (7 of the 12 still open) were open at that step on 2026-01-20, and they had sat there longest, 4 to 41 days (median 16). In the 12 finished setups, Connect calendar was also the step left open longest in 8 of 12.
[MEDIUM] (stall at Invite your team) Invite your team is the second most common stopping point: 3 of 24 setups started (3 of the 12 still open), open 6, 11 and 19 days.
[LOW] (other steps) 1 of 24 was open at Practice details (5 days) and 1 of 24 at Review & finish (2 days). No setup was open at Sign in, because a setup only counts as started once someone has signed in.
Representative Quotes
None — this session has no participants.
Recommendations
Run a moderated usability test of the setup flow with both Practice Administrators and IT Administrators, focused on Connect calendar and Invite your team, to find out why setups stop there.
Ask the dashboard owners whether the signed-in person's role can be shown per setup, so later reviews can tell Practice Administrator setups from IT Administrator ones.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why do setups stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team? A dashboard can't show reasons: it records where a setup is open and for how long, not what the person at that step was thinking or waiting for.
Do stopped setups eventually finish, or are they abandoned? Re-check these 12 open setups at the next review.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

sources.title: Dashboard review — Compass AI practice setup completion
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the Compass AI practice setup flow, the flow a practice's administrator uses to set Compass AI up for their practice, to see where setups stop and how long they stay stopped. This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training. The dashboard records setups, not why a practice started one or which Compass AI features it was setting up for, and the corpus doesn't record how practices were chosen to set up or when each planned to go live. This review is not tied to the ambient scribe GA: the GA candidate was still under test on 2026-01-13 ( 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ).
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal usage dashboard for the practice setup flow, covering setups started 2025-12-01 to 2026-01-16 (seven weeks), with step status as of the review date, 2026-01-20
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Context: The flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, 5 Review & finish. Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it. A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20. The dashboard shows setups by practice; it doesn't show the signed-in person's role, so whether a Practice Administrator or an IT Administrator ran each setup isn't known. The number of practices in the network isn't on the dashboard and isn't recorded in the corpus, so no completion rate against all practices is given here.
Counts (24 setups started in the window):
Finished (completed Review & finish): 12 of 24
Still open on 2026-01-20: 12 of 24, stopped at:
Practice details: 1 of 24, open 5 days
Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)
Invite your team: 3 of 24, open 6, 11 and 19 days
Review & finish: 1 of 24, open 2 days
Reached Review & finish: 13 of 24 (the 12 finished plus the 1 still open there)
Key Findings
[HIGH] (stall at Connect calendar) Connect calendar is where setups stop most: 7 of the 24 setups started (7 of the 12 still open) were open at that step on 2026-01-20, and they had sat there longest, 4 to 41 days (median 16). In the 12 finished setups, Connect calendar was also the step left open longest in 8 of 12.
[MEDIUM] (stall at Invite your team) Invite your team is the second most common stopping point: 3 of 24 setups started (3 of the 12 still open), open 6, 11 and 19 days.
[LOW] (other steps) 1 of 24 was open at Practice details (5 days) and 1 of 24 at Review & finish (2 days). No setup was open at Sign in, because a setup only counts as started once someone has signed in.
Representative Quotes
None — this session has no participants.
Recommendations
Run a moderated usability test of the setup flow with both Practice Administrators and IT Administrators, focused on Connect calendar and Invite your team, to find out why setups stop there.
Ask the dashboard owners whether the signed-in person's role can be shown per setup, so later reviews can tell Practice Administrator setups from IT Administrator ones.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why do setups stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team? A dashboard can't show reasons: it records where a setup is open and for how long, not what the person at that step was thinking or waiting for.
Do stopped setups eventually finish, or are they abandoned? Re-check these 12 open setups at the next review.

sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1

Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

questions.question: What did nurses want from the citations in the prior auth drafts?

seeded.answer: Nurses wanted to see inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion, describing this as “show your work” [1][2]. Specifically, 3 of 4 participants in the April 2025 v1 test requested this feature [1]. One participant in a September 2026 interview stated, “I’ve never had a draft without them. The citations aren’t extra, they’re how I read the thing” [3]. They don’t just want to know the citation exists, but whether the cited text supports the wording of the draft [3]. Nurses in the pilot program open the citations for the diagnosis and the date of the most recent supporting note on every case, and skim the rest [4]. They check dates first due to a previous issue with outdated diagnosis codes [4].

sources.title: Usability Test — AI-Assisted Prior Authorization Drafting (v1)
sources.participants: Participants: 4 — Utilization Review Nurse, Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor)
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Test whether an AI-drafted prior authorization request (pulling from chart data to pre-fill medical necessity justification) speeds up the process without introducing errors that could cause denials.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 4 realistic case scenarios, 60 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (accuracy) In 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes still present elsewhere in the chart rather than the most recent/active ones, which participants said would likely cause a payer denial if submitted as-is.
[HIGH] (liability concern) The supervisor was firm that nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission, since a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care by days — no shortcut is acceptable here.
[HIGH] (time savings (positive)) Despite the above, participants estimated the draft cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct, which was seen as a real win if accuracy improves.
[MEDIUM] (transparency) Participants wanted to see which specific chart entries the AI pulled from, inline, rather than trusting a black-box summary — 'show your work' was mentioned unprompted by 3 of 4.
Representative Quotes
"Five minutes saved is great until it's the case that gets denied and now I'm on the phone with the payer for 40 minutes instead. Show me where it got that info." — Utilization Review Nurse, P17
"I actually really liked this for the boring, obvious cases. Just don't let it near the complicated ones yet." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19
Recommendations
Fix the outdated-diagnosis-code issue before any further piloting; this is a correctness bug, not a UX issue.
Add inline source citations (chart entry + date) for every claim in the generated justification.
Consider limiting initial pilot scope to 'straightforward' case types the nurses themselves can help define, deferring complex cases.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Work with engineering to confirm whether the outdated-code issue is a data-freshness bug or a model retrieval issue.
Ask supervisor to help define what counts as a 'straightforward' case for a narrower v2 pilot scope.
Correction (2026-10-13)
Filed 2026-10-13 as correction-2026-10-13.md in this session's folder. The original notes above are unchanged.
Corrects session-notes.md in this folder. That file is left unedited ( raw/ is append-only).

sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). Both claims come from the April 2025 v1 and November 2025 v2 tests, whose participants asked for the citations or tested them. This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.
Representative Quotes
"I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
"A denial comes with a reason, and the reason's in the letter, not the chart. So I start from the letter and go find what answers it." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, note that the citation requirement holds for a nurse who joined during the pilot, and that what they check is whether the cited text supports the draft's wording.
If citation use is measured in the pilot, record what nurses check in a citation, not only whether they open one.
Ask the pilot team whether a submitted request keeps its citations, so a nurse can reuse them if the health plan asks about the case later.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

sources.title: Interview — Returning Utilization Review Nurse on Pilot Case Scope
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P19 — Utilization Review Nurse (nurse), returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1 ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Check the prior-auth scope decision in prior-authorization.md against daily work, with a nurse who now uses the drafting panel. The finding says scope discipline held: pilot scope was limited to "straightforward" cases and complex cases were kept out ( findings/prior-authorization.md :35-38), and that inline citations are actively used rather than ignored (lines 32-34). Both rest on test sessions with realistic scenarios. The participant is P19, returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1, where they said they liked the draft "for the boring, obvious cases" and wanted it kept away from complicated ones. The questions were whether the straightforward boundary matches the cases that actually reach them, how they check the panel's citations, and which cases they still do by hand.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only, the scope the v2 test recommended (2025-11-04-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v2/session-notes.md:39). Complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant is in the pilot and uses the panel on their own straightforward cases. They took part in the April 2025 v1 test only, not the November 2025 v2 test, so nothing here speaks to v2. They are not P17, the utilization review supervisor quoted in v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either; what the participant says about it is their own description.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (boundary vs case mix) The boundary holds as a rule but does not sort their cases cleanly up front. In their own words, a straightforward case is "one request, one current diagnosis, criteria we see every week." On their informal estimate, roughly half of what reaches them in a week looks like that at intake, and some of those turn out not to be once they are into the chart: an older related request, a prior claim denial on the same service, or evidence spread over years of notes. When that happens they stop using the draft and finish the case by hand, so the decision is made case by case, partway through, by the nurse. This complicates the finding's "scope discipline held" claim: the scope held in testing, where cases were labelled straightforward or complex in advance, but in daily work the label is not known until the nurse has read enough of the chart.
[MEDIUM] (citation checking) They open the citations for the diagnosis and for the date of the most recent supporting note on every case, and skim the rest. They check dates first because of the outdated-code issue they saw in v1. They said they have not seen an outdated code in the pilot; that is their account, not a count, and v2's no-recurrence result covered 4 test cases. This confirms the finding's claim that citations are used rather than ignored, and extends it from a test session to one nurse's daily use; it says nothing about how other pilot users check.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases) Cases they still do entirely by hand: anything following a prior claim denial, requests covering several services at once, and cases with long histories where they have to judge which evidence matters. Their reason was the same for all three: the work is deciding what to include, and a draft that includes things they then have to remove is slower than starting blank. Their rule when unsure is to treat the case as complex.
Representative Quotes
"The definition's fine on paper. The trouble is a lot of my cases look straightforward right up until I'm into the chart." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
"I click the dates first. After the old-codes problem last year, I don't trust a diagnosis until I've seen when it was written." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, say that the straightforward boundary is applied by the nurse during the case, not only at intake, and that cases leave the draft partway through.
Treat a case that starts in the panel and moves to manual as a normal path, and ask the pilot team whether it is recorded, since it is part of what the pilot is testing.
Keep dates prominent in the citations; this nurse checks them before anything else.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, and none was reviewed here. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
What "pilot expansion" in the v2 recommendation meant (how many nurses, how many weeks, what go/no-go metric) is still the open question v2 left; this participant did not know, and was not in v2.
How often a case leaves the draft partway through is not measured; "roughly half" looking straightforward at intake is one nurse's estimate.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.

The citations aren’t extra, they’re how I read the thing” [3]. sources.participants: Participants: 4 — Utilization Review Nurse, Utilization Review Nurse (supervisor)
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Test whether an AI-drafted prior authorization request (pulling from chart data to pre-fill medical necessity justification) speeds up the process without introducing errors that could cause denials.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 4 realistic case scenarios, 60 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (accuracy) In 2 of 4 cases, the AI draft cited outdated diagnosis codes still present elsewhere in the chart rather than the most recent/active ones, which participants said would likely cause a payer denial if submitted as-is.
[HIGH] (liability concern) The supervisor was firm that nurses would still need to read every AI-drafted justification in full before submission, since a wrongly submitted prior auth can delay patient care by days — no shortcut is acceptable here.
[HIGH] (time savings (positive)) Despite the above, participants estimated the draft cut initial drafting time from ~15 minutes to ~5 minutes per straightforward case when the citation was correct, which was seen as a real win if accuracy improves.
[MEDIUM] (transparency) Participants wanted to see which specific chart entries the AI pulled from, inline, rather than trusting a black-box summary — 'show your work' was mentioned unprompted by 3 of 4.
Representative Quotes
"Five minutes saved is great until it's the case that gets denied and now I'm on the phone with the payer for 40 minutes instead. Show me where it got that info." — Utilization Review Nurse, P17
"I actually really liked this for the boring, obvious cases. Just don't let it near the complicated ones yet." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19
Recommendations
Fix the outdated-diagnosis-code issue before any further piloting; this is a correctness bug, not a UX issue.
Add inline source citations (chart entry + date) for every claim in the generated justification.
Consider limiting initial pilot scope to 'straightforward' case types the nurses themselves can help define, deferring complex cases.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Work with engineering to confirm whether the outdated-code issue is a data-freshness bug or a model retrieval issue.
Ask supervisor to help define what counts as a 'straightforward' case for a narrower v2 pilot scope.
Correction (2026-10-13)
Filed 2026-10-13 as correction-2026-10-13.md in this session's folder. The original notes above are unchanged.

sources.title: AI-Assisted Prior Authorization
sources.excerpt:
AI-drafted prior authorization justifications were tested in two rounds (v1, Apr 2025; v2, Nov 2025) with the same utilization review nurse supervisor across both, which mattered for tracking whether fixes actually landed.
v1 surfaced a correctness bug (citing outdated diagnosis codes) serious enough that participants said it would likely cause payer denials — not a UX problem, a data-freshness/model fix. It also surfaced a durable requirement: nurses want inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion ("show your work"), not just a black-box draft.

sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). Both claims come from the April 2025 v1 and November 2025 v2 tests, whose participants asked for the citations or tested them. This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. They use the panel on their own straightforward cases. They are not P19, the utilization review nurse from v1 and June 2026, and not P17, the utilization review supervisor from v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either.
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (citations as the way to read a draft) They want the citations, and don't think of them as an added feature: they have never used a draft without them, and opening them is how they read a draft at all. On each case they open the citation behind every criterion the request has to meet and read the chart entry it points to. What they check is whether that entry says what the draft says it says, not only that it exists; their example was a cited note that supports a symptom the draft describes as ongoing, when the note is months old. On their informal impression, most drafts need no change after checking and some need a sentence reworded; they kept no count. This confirms prior-authorization.md :30-34 for a nurse who wasn't in v1 or v2: the citations are wanted and used in pilot work, not only in testing. It also complicates the v2 measure: "clicked into at least one citation" records that a citation was opened, not what the nurse checked once it was.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases, claim denials and calls) Cases outside the pilot's straightforward scope they do by hand from the start. For a request that follows a claim denial, they begin from the denial letter's stated reason and then gather the chart evidence that answers it; in their view a draft built from the chart would start in the wrong place, because the reason is in the letter, not the chart. Before a call with the health plan about a case, they prepare by hand too, keeping their own list of chart references to have open during the call. They described the calls as the hardest part of the week to plan for, but gave no time figure. For a straightforward case that the health plan later asks about, they said they find the evidence again from scratch; they didn't know whether a submitted request keeps the panel's citations.
Representative Quotes
"I've never had a draft without them. The citations aren't extra, they're how I read the thing." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
"A denial comes with a reason, and the reason's in the letter, not the chart. So I start from the letter and go find what answers it." — Utilization Review Nurse, P144
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, note that the citation requirement holds for a nurse who joined during the pilot, and that what they check is whether the cited text supports the draft's wording.
If citation use is measured in the pilot, record what nurses check in a citation, not only whether they open one.
Ask the pilot team whether a submitted request keeps its citations, so a nurse can reuse them if the health plan asks about the case later.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, none was reviewed here, and the participant had not seen any figures. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
Whether a submitted request keeps its citations is not known; the participant didn't know.
How many drafts need changing after the citations are checked is not counted; "most" needing no change is one nurse's impression.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.
Whether drafting could help with requests that follow a claim denial is untested; the participant does them by hand, and nothing here supports bringing them into the pilot.

sources.title: Interview — Returning Utilization Review Nurse on Pilot Case Scope
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P19 — Utilization Review Nurse (nurse), returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1 ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Check the prior-auth scope decision in prior-authorization.md against daily work, with a nurse who now uses the drafting panel. The finding says scope discipline held: pilot scope was limited to "straightforward" cases and complex cases were kept out ( findings/prior-authorization.md :35-38), and that inline citations are actively used rather than ignored (lines 32-34). Both rest on test sessions with realistic scenarios. The participant is P19, returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1, where they said they liked the draft "for the boring, obvious cases" and wanted it kept away from complicated ones. The questions were whether the straightforward boundary matches the cases that actually reach them, how they check the panel's citations, and which cases they still do by hand.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only, the scope the v2 test recommended (2025-11-04-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v2/session-notes.md:39). Complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant is in the pilot and uses the panel on their own straightforward cases. They took part in the April 2025 v1 test only, not the November 2025 v2 test, so nothing here speaks to v2. They are not P17, the utilization review supervisor quoted in v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either; what the participant says about it is their own description.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (boundary vs case mix) The boundary holds as a rule but does not sort their cases cleanly up front. In their own words, a straightforward case is "one request, one current diagnosis, criteria we see every week." On their informal estimate, roughly half of what reaches them in a week looks like that at intake, and some of those turn out not to be once they are into the chart: an older related request, a prior claim denial on the same service, or evidence spread over years of notes. When that happens they stop using the draft and finish the case by hand, so the decision is made case by case, partway through, by the nurse. This complicates the finding's "scope discipline held" claim: the scope held in testing, where cases were labelled straightforward or complex in advance, but in daily work the label is not known until the nurse has read enough of the chart.
[MEDIUM] (citation checking) They open the citations for the diagnosis and for the date of the most recent supporting note on every case, and skim the rest. They check dates first because of the outdated-code issue they saw in v1. They said they have not seen an outdated code in the pilot; that is their account, not a count, and v2's no-recurrence result covered 4 test cases. This confirms the finding's claim that citations are used rather than ignored, and extends it from a test session to one nurse's daily use; it says nothing about how other pilot users check.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases) Cases they still do entirely by hand: anything following a prior claim denial, requests covering several services at once, and cases with long histories where they have to judge which evidence matters. Their reason was the same for all three: the work is deciding what to include, and a draft that includes things they then have to remove is slower than starting blank. Their rule when unsure is to treat the case as complex.
Representative Quotes
"The definition's fine on paper. The trouble is a lot of my cases look straightforward right up until I'm into the chart." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
"I click the dates first. After the old-codes problem last year, I don't trust a diagnosis until I've seen when it was written." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, say that the straightforward boundary is applied by the nurse during the case, not only at intake, and that cases leave the draft partway through.
Treat a case that starts in the panel and moves to manual as a normal path, and ask the pilot team whether it is recorded, since it is part of what the pilot is testing.
Keep dates prominent in the citations; this nurse checks them before anything else.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, and none was reviewed here. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
What "pilot expansion" in the v2 recommendation meant (how many nurses, how many weeks, what go/no-go metric) is still the open question v2 left; this participant did not know, and was not in v2.
How often a case leaves the draft partway through is not measured; "roughly half" looking straightforward at intake is one nurse's estimate.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.

Nurses wanted to see inline citations to the specific chart text behind each suggestion, describing this as “show your work” [1][2]. Specifically, 3 of 4 participants in the April 2025 v1 test requested this feature [1]. One participant in a September 2026 interview stated, “I’ve never had a draft without them. The citations aren’t extra, they’re how I read the thing” [3]. sources.title: Interview — Utilization Review Nurse on Checking Citations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
prior-authorization.md says nurses want inline citations to the chart text behind each part of the draft, and that in v2 the citations were used rather than ignored, with 3 of 4 participants clicking into at least one citation before accepting ( findings/prior-authorization.md :30-34). Both claims come from the April 2025 v1 and November 2025 v2 tests, whose participants asked for the citations or tested them. This session asked a utilization review nurse who joined the department after both tests, and has only ever used the panel in the pilot, whether they want the citations and how they check them, and how they handle the cases the panel doesn't take, including claim denials and calls with the health plan.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only; complex cases stay manual. The participant joined the department after the November 2025 v2 test and did not take part in any earlier session, so nothing here speaks to v1 or v2. sources.title: Interview — Returning Utilization Review Nurse on Pilot Case Scope
sources.participants: Participants: 1 — P19 — Utilization Review Nurse (nurse), returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1 ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Check the prior-auth scope decision in prior-authorization.md against daily work, with a nurse who now uses the drafting panel. The finding says scope discipline held: pilot scope was limited to "straightforward" cases and complex cases were kept out ( findings/prior-authorization.md :35-38), and that inline citations are actively used rather than ignored (lines 32-34). Both rest on test sessions with realistic scenarios. The participant is P19, returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1, where they said they liked the draft "for the boring, obvious cases" and wanted it kept away from complicated ones. The questions were whether the straightforward boundary matches the cases that actually reach them, how they check the panel's citations, and which cases they still do by hand.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: A limited pilot of the prior-auth drafting panel has run in the utilization review department since early 2026, on straightforward cases only, the scope the v2 test recommended (2025-11-04-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v2/session-notes.md:39). Complex cases stay manual. The pilot is not generally available and has not reached other departments. The panel shows inline citations to the chart entries behind each part of the draft. The participant is in the pilot and uses the panel on their own straightforward cases. They took part in the April 2025 v1 test only, not the November 2025 v2 test, so nothing here speaks to v2. They are not P17, the utilization review supervisor quoted in v1 and v2. No pilot outcomes data was reviewed in this session, and the written straightforward-case definition was not reviewed either; what the participant says about it is their own description.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (boundary vs case mix) The boundary holds as a rule but does not sort their cases cleanly up front. In their own words, a straightforward case is "one request, one current diagnosis, criteria we see every week." On their informal estimate, roughly half of what reaches them in a week looks like that at intake, and some of those turn out not to be once they are into the chart: an older related request, a prior claim denial on the same service, or evidence spread over years of notes. When that happens they stop using the draft and finish the case by hand, so the decision is made case by case, partway through, by the nurse. This complicates the finding's "scope discipline held" claim: the scope held in testing, where cases were labelled straightforward or complex in advance, but in daily work the label is not known until the nurse has read enough of the chart.
[MEDIUM] (citation checking) They open the citations for the diagnosis and for the date of the most recent supporting note on every case, and skim the rest. They check dates first because of the outdated-code issue they saw in v1. They said they have not seen an outdated code in the pilot; that is their account, not a count, and v2's no-recurrence result covered 4 test cases. This confirms the finding's claim that citations are used rather than ignored, and extends it from a test session to one nurse's daily use; it says nothing about how other pilot users check.
[MEDIUM] (manual cases) Cases they still do entirely by hand: anything following a prior claim denial, requests covering several services at once, and cases with long histories where they have to judge which evidence matters. Their reason was the same for all three: the work is deciding what to include, and a draft that includes things they then have to remove is slower than starting blank. Their rule when unsure is to treat the case as complex.
Representative Quotes
"The definition's fine on paper. The trouble is a lot of my cases look straightforward right up until I'm into the chart." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
"I click the dates first. After the old-codes problem last year, I don't trust a diagnosis until I've seen when it was written." — Utilization Review Nurse, P19 (returning from 2025-04-08-usability-test-prior-auth-ai-v1)
Recommendations
When prior-authorization.md is next revised, say that the straightforward boundary is applied by the nurse during the case, not only at intake, and that cases leave the draft partway through.
Treat a case that starts in the panel and moves to manual as a normal path, and ask the pilot team whether it is recorded, since it is part of what the pilot is testing.
Keep dates prominent in the citations; this nurse checks them before anything else.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How the pilot is performing is not known: no outcomes data (time, accuracy, claim denials) is recorded in the corpus, and none was reviewed here. The only time figures on record are v1's estimate and v2's measurement on 2 straightforward test cases.
What "pilot expansion" in the v2 recommendation meant (how many nurses, how many weeks, what go/no-go metric) is still the open question v2 left; this participant did not know, and was not in v2.
How often a case leaves the draft partway through is not measured; "roughly half" looking straightforward at intake is one nurse's estimate.
Whether other pilot users check citations the same way is not known; this is one interview.

The citations aren’t extra, they’re how I read the thing” [3]. They don’t just want to know the citation exists, but whether the cited text supports the wording of the draft [3]. questions.question: How were sound-alike medication names handled?

seeded.answer:
The sources detail a multi-stage approach to handling sound-alike medication names. Initially, the system flagged potential sound-alike errors with a low-confidence underline, identifying dosage errors and sound-alike names in earlier versions [1]. A concept for a distinct sound-alike medication flag was tested with 6 participants – 5 of 6 correctly identified it as different from the standard low-confidence underline [2]. However, the test also revealed that 2 participants might over-trust unflagged medication lines, assuming they were automatically correct [2][3].

The physician interviewed on March 24, 2026, recalled one instance of a sound-alike name (glyburide instead of glipizide) since the January 2026 GA, which was underlined [1]. They stated they check every medication line against the order, regardless of marking, because a wrong name can be confidently presented [1]. The distinct medication flag had not shipped at the time of the interview [1]. A later interview with an infusion nurse revealed they had not seen any marking on medication lines in signed notes, and assumed providers had already checked them [4]. The design of the flag included an amber pill-shaped badge placed inline with the medication name, prompted verification with a hover label ("verify before signing"), and was visually distinct from the low-confidence underline [5].

Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min

Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.
