sources.title: Interview — Infusion Nurse on Medication Changes in Scribe-Drafted Notes
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The medication thread in ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinements.md rests on a concept test of a distinct sound-alike medication flag with the people who review and sign scribe drafts: physicians and NPs (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/participants.md). Nobody who reads a signed, scribe-drafted note and then gives the medication has been asked about it. This session asked an infusion nurse how they check medication changes in the treating provider's visit note before they administer, and what, if anything, they see on medication lines in a signed note.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a registered nurse in an ambulatory infusion clinic, mid-career. Patients come in for scheduled infusions, and before starting one the nurse checks the infusion order against the treating provider's most recent visit note, which since the January 2026 GA is often scribe-drafted. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs only; the participant doesn't use it, and their own charting is manual. They did not take part in any earlier session. They are not P138, the primary care clinic nurse interviewed in March 2026, and they don't do care coordination or post-discharge calls. The distinct medication flag is recorded in the corpus as a concept test (2026-02-10) and a wireframe in review ( wireframes/ambient-scribe-medication-flag.md ), whose hover copy reads "verify before signing"; nothing was shown in this session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (checking before administering) Before every infusion they compare the order with the treating provider's latest visit note, looking for a medication change: a changed dose, a held infusion, a premedication added or stopped, or a lab value that has to be checked first. They give the medication from the order, not the note; the note is how they find out whether the order still reflects what was decided at the visit. When the two disagree, they hold the infusion and contact the provider before starting. In scribe-drafted notes they sometimes find a change in the body of the note, written up from the conversation, rather than in the plan, or worded so that they can't tell whether it was decided ("we'll probably bring the dose down"). They recalled holding an infusion to check for this reason "maybe once or twice a month" since GA; that is an informal recollection, not a count, and they couldn't say how many of those came from the scribe's drafting and how many from the provider. This is the same pattern of plan items landing in the body that the March 2026 clinic nurse described (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes/session-notes.md:30), in a different setting: here the cost is a delayed infusion before administration, not a delayed callback.
[MEDIUM] (the flag and readers) The medication flag has so far been designed and tested for the person signing the note. This nurse reads the note after it is signed and acts on its medication lines. In the signed notes they read, they said they have not seen any marking on medication lines, neither a flag nor an underline; that is what they see, not a statement of how the product behaves. Their working assumption is that every medication line in a signed note was checked by the provider. That is a reader's version of the over-trust risk the concept test found in 2 of 6 signers, who trusted unflagged lines more: a reader who never sees a flag treats every signed line as checked. They said that if a line had been flagged and the provider then confirmed or changed it, they would want to know, because that is the line they would check against the order first. That is an expectation; no such view exists. This extends the medication-flag finding to readers who didn't write the note.
Representative Quotes
"I don't hang anything off the note, I hang it off the order. The note is how I find out if the order's still right." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
"If it's signed, I assume they checked the meds. I've never seen anything on a med line that tells me different." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that medication changes decided at the visit need to reach the plan section as decided changes, because infusion nurses check them against the order before administering.
When the medication flag's design is next reviewed, include nurses who read signed notes and give the medication as a user group, and decide explicitly whether anything about a flag, and what the signer did with it, should reach them. Don't assume either answer.
Keep this evidence separate from the care coordination evidence on after-visit summaries: this is the visit note checked against the order before administration, not the summary a patient takes home.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Whether the medication flag, or any confidence marking, stays visible after a note is signed is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here. This nurse has not seen any marking on signed notes, which says what they see, not how the product behaves; and the corpus records the distinct flag only as a concept test and a wireframe in review.
How often an infusion is held because the note and the order disagree is not measured; "once or twice a month" is one nurse's recollection, and how many of those trace back to scribe drafting is not known.
Whether other infusion nurses, or nurses in other clinics, check the note against the order the same way is not known; this is one interview.
How often the after-visit summary misses medication changes remains open in the care coordination evidence; it was not discussed here.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.

Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.

"I put the order in myself, so I know what I decided. The question is whether the note says the same thing." — Physician (Family Medicine), P147

When the distinct medication flag's design is next reviewed, note that this physician checks every medication line against the order regardless of marking; whether a flag would change that is untested.

How often plan items land outside the plan section is not measured; "a couple of times on a full clinic day" is one physician's impression.

Whether the distinct medication flag would change how signers check medication lines is untested; it has not shipped.

sources.title: Usability Test — Ambient Scribe Sound-Alike Medication Flag Concept
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The GA-candidate round (2026-01-13) recommended treating sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing post-GA monitoring item rather than a launch blocker, since the existing confidence-highlighted variant already surfaces them as generically low-confidence. This session tests an early concept that goes one step further: a distinct flag specifically for suspected sound-alike medication names, visually separate from the general low-confidence underline, to see whether participants notice and act on it differently than they do on ordinary low-confidence text.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, 6 simulated encounters seeded with known sound-alike pairs (e.g. hydralazine/hydroxyzine, clonidine/Klonopin), 40 min/session
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (flag recognized correctly) 5 of 6 participants correctly identified the medication-specific flag (a distinct amber pill-shaped badge, vs. the generic low-confidence underline) as "different from the usual low-confidence thing" within the first two encounters, without being told the distinction existed.
[MEDIUM] (over-trust risk) 2 participants said the badge's specificity made them more likely to treat unflagged medication lines as automatically correct — the opposite of the intended effect, and worth watching as adoption scales.
[LOW] (placement) Badge placement inline with the medication name (vs. in a right-hand margin, tested as an alternate) was preferred 5:1 — participants didn't want to look away from the text to check a flag.
[LOW] (false positive tolerance) One deliberately-seeded false positive (a real but unusual drug name) was accepted by all 6 participants as "worth a second look, not annoying" — suggests some over-flagging is tolerable if the badge is visually light.
Representative Quotes
"That's different from the fuzzy-underline stuff — this one's telling me specifically 'check the drug name,' which is exactly what I'd want flagged." — Physician, Internal Medicine, P22
"If it's not flagged, I might just... trust it more than I should. That's on me, but it's worth knowing the tool does that to people." — Nurse Practitioner, P24
Recommendations
Build the distinct medication-safety flag as its own variant, inline with the medication name, separate from generic confidence highlighting.
Before rollout, pair the flag with brief onboarding copy or training-pilot messaging that explicitly counters the over-trust-on-unflagged-lines risk surfaced by 2 of 6 participants — don't let the flag imply "anything unflagged is guaranteed correct."
Feed the false-positive tolerance finding to whoever tunes the sound-alike detection threshold — participants have headroom for a few extra false positives in exchange for not missing a real one.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Needs a larger-N validation pass before this moves from concept test to build-ready spec.
Over-trust-on-unflagged risk should be checked again once the post-GA monitoring dashboard (recommended 2026-01-13) has real error-rate data to compare against self-reported behavior.

sources.excerpt: In a 6-person concept test, a distinct sound-alike-medication flag was recognized as different from generic confidence highlighting. The GA-candidate round treated sound-alike medication errors as an ongoing monitoring item, relying on the general confidence-highlighted variant to surface them. A concept test of a dedicated, visually distinct flag found 5 of 6 participants correctly recognized it as categorically different from generic low confidence — but also surfaced a new risk: 2 of 6 participants said the flag's specificity made them trust unflagged medication lines more than they should. Any rollout needs to actively counter that over-trust framing, not just ship the flag.

sources.title: Interview — Infusion Nurse on Medication Changes in Scribe-Drafted Notes
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The medication thread in ambient-scribe-post-ga-refinements.md rests on a concept test of a distinct sound-alike medication flag with the people who review and sign scribe drafts: physicians and NPs (2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/participants.md). Nobody who reads a signed, scribe-drafted note and then gives the medication has been asked about it. This session asked an infusion nurse how they check medication changes in the treating provider's visit note before they administer, and what, if anything, they see on medication lines in a signed note.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a registered nurse in an ambulatory infusion clinic, mid-career. Patients come in for scheduled infusions, and before starting one the nurse checks the infusion order against the treating provider's most recent visit note, which since the January 2026 GA is often scribe-drafted. The scribe drafts visit notes for physicians, NPs and PAs only; the participant doesn't use it, and their own charting is manual. They did not take part in any earlier session. They are not P138, the primary care clinic nurse interviewed in March 2026, and they don't do care coordination or post-discharge calls. The distinct medication flag is recorded in the corpus as a concept test (2026-02-10) and a wireframe in review ( wireframes/ambient-scribe-medication-flag.md ), whose hover copy reads "verify before signing"; nothing was shown in this session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (checking before administering) Before every infusion they compare the order with the treating provider's latest visit note, looking for a medication change: a changed dose, a held infusion, a premedication added or stopped, or a lab value that has to be checked first. They give the medication from the order, not the note; the note is how they find out whether the order still reflects what was decided at the visit. When the two disagree, they hold the infusion and contact the provider before starting. In scribe-drafted notes they sometimes find a change in the body of the note, written up from the conversation, rather than in the plan, or worded so that they can't tell whether it was decided ("we'll probably bring the dose down"). They recalled holding an infusion to check for this reason "maybe once or twice a month" since GA; that is an informal recollection, not a count, and they couldn't say how many of those came from the scribe's drafting and how many from the provider. This is the same pattern of plan items landing in the body that the March 2026 clinic nurse described (2026-03-17-interview-clinic-nurse-reading-scribe-drafted-notes/session-notes.md:30), in a different setting: here the cost is a delayed infusion before administration, not a delayed callback.
[MEDIUM] (the flag and readers) The medication flag has so far been designed and tested for the person signing the note. This nurse reads the note after it is signed and acts on its medication lines. In the signed notes they read, they said they have not seen any marking on medication lines, neither a flag nor an underline; that is what they see, not a statement of how the product behaves. Their working assumption is that every medication line in a signed note was checked by the provider. That is a reader's version of the over-trust risk the concept test found in 2 of 6 signers, who trusted unflagged lines more: a reader who never sees a flag treats every signed line as checked. They said that if a line had been flagged and the provider then confirmed or changed it, they would want to know, because that is the line they would check against the order first. That is an expectation; no such view exists. This extends the medication-flag finding to readers who didn't write the note.
Representative Quotes
"I don't hang anything off the note, I hang it off the order. The note is how I find out if the order's still right." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
"If it's signed, I assume they checked the meds. I've never seen anything on a med line that tells me different." — Registered Nurse (infusion clinic), P143
Recommendations
Share with the ambient scribe team that medication changes decided at the visit need to reach the plan section as decided changes, because infusion nurses check them against the order before administering.
When the medication flag's design is next reviewed, include nurses who read signed notes and give the medication as a user group, and decide explicitly whether anything about a flag, and what the signer did with it, should reach them. Don't assume either answer.
Keep this evidence separate from the care coordination evidence on after-visit summaries: this is the visit note checked against the order before administration, not the summary a patient takes home.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Whether the medication flag, or any confidence marking, stays visible after a note is signed is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here. This nurse has not seen any marking on signed notes, which says what they see, not how the product behaves; and the corpus records the distinct flag only as a concept test and a wireframe in review.
How often an infusion is held because the note and the order disagree is not measured; "once or twice a month" is one nurse's recollection, and how many of those trace back to scribe drafting is not known.
Whether other infusion nurses, or nurses in other clinics, check the note against the order the same way is not known; this is one interview.
How often the after-visit summary misses medication changes remains open in the care coordination evidence; it was not discussed here.

questions.question: List the onboarding steps in order.

seeded.answer:
The Compass AI practice setup flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, and 5 Review & finish [1][2]. Every step is required and cannot be skipped, only left open [1]. A setup is considered started when someone signs in at step 1 and stopped when it remains open at a step [1][2].

The usability test and dashboard review focused on steps 3 and 4 because these are where setups stall most frequently [2][3][4]. Specifically, 7 of 24 setups started were open at “Connect calendar” and 3 of 24 were open at “Invite your team” as of January 20, 2026 [2].

The research identified that 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at “Connect calendar” because they believed IT should approve access to the appointment schedule [3]. IT Administrators also asked which fields would be read from the calendar before connecting [3]. At “Invite your team”, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators hesitated, concerned about emailing staff before training was scheduled [3].

sources.title: Dashboard review — Compass AI practice setup completion
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the Compass AI practice setup flow, the flow a practice's administrator uses to set Compass AI up for their practice, to see where setups stop and how long they stay stopped. This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training. The dashboard records setups, not why a practice started one or which Compass AI features it was setting up for, and the corpus doesn't record how practices were chosen to set up or when each planned to go live. This review is not tied to the ambient scribe GA: the GA candidate was still under test on 2026-01-13 ( 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ).
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal usage dashboard for the practice setup flow, covering setups started 2025-12-01 to 2026-01-16 (seven weeks), with step status as of the review date, 2026-01-20
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Context: The flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, 5 Review & finish. Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it. A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20. The dashboard shows setups by practice; it doesn't show the signed-in person's role, so whether a Practice Administrator or an IT Administrator ran each setup isn't known. The number of practices in the network isn't on the dashboard and isn't recorded in the corpus, so no completion rate against all practices is given here.
Counts (24 setups started in the window):
Finished (completed Review & finish): 12 of 24
Still open on 2026-01-20: 12 of 24, stopped at:
Practice details: 1 of 24, open 5 days
Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)
Invite your team: 3 of 24, open 6, 11 and 19 days
Review & finish: 1 of 24, open 2 days
Reached Review & finish: 13 of 24 (the 12 finished plus the 1 still open there)
Key Findings
[HIGH] (stall at Connect calendar) Connect calendar is where setups stop most: 7 of the 24 setups started (7 of the 12 still open) were open at that step on 2026-01-20, and they had sat there longest, 4 to 41 days (median 16). In the 12 finished setups, Connect calendar was also the step left open longest in 8 of 12.
[MEDIUM] (stall at Invite your team) Invite your team is the second most common stopping point: 3 of 24 setups started (3 of the 12 still open), open 6, 11 and 19 days.
[LOW] (other steps) 1 of 24 was open at Practice details (5 days) and 1 of 24 at Review & finish (2 days). No setup was open at Sign in, because a setup only counts as started once someone has signed in.
Representative Quotes
None — this session has no participants.
Recommendations
Run a moderated usability test of the setup flow with both Practice Administrators and IT Administrators, focused on Connect calendar and Invite your team, to find out why setups stop there.
Ask the dashboard owners whether the signed-in person's role can be shown per setup, so later reviews can tell Practice Administrator setups from IT Administrator ones.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why do setups stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team? A dashboard can't show reasons: it records where a setup is open and for how long, not what the person at that step was thinking or waiting for.
Do stopped setups eventually finish, or are they abandoned? Re-check these 12 open setups at the next review.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)

None — this session has no participants.

sources.title: Dashboard review — Compass AI practice setup completion
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the Compass AI practice setup flow, the flow a practice's administrator uses to set Compass AI up for their practice, to see where setups stop and how long they stay stopped. This is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training. The dashboard records setups, not why a practice started one or which Compass AI features it was setting up for, and the corpus doesn't record how practices were chosen to set up or when each planned to go live. This review is not tied to the ambient scribe GA: the GA candidate was still under test on 2026-01-13 ( 2026-01-13-usability-test-ambient-scribe-ga-release-candidate ).
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal usage dashboard for the practice setup flow, covering setups started 2025-12-01 to 2026-01-16 (seven weeks), with step status as of the review date, 2026-01-20
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Context: The flow has five steps: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO, 2 Practice details, 3 Connect calendar, 4 Invite your team, 5 Review & finish. Every step is required in this build; a setup can't skip a step, it can only be left open at it. A setup counts as started when someone signs in at step 1. "Stopped" means the setup was still open at that step on 2026-01-20. The dashboard shows setups by practice; it doesn't show the signed-in person's role, so whether a Practice Administrator or an IT Administrator ran each setup isn't known. The number of practices in the network isn't on the dashboard and isn't recorded in the corpus, so no completion rate against all practices is given here.
Counts (24 setups started in the window):
Finished (completed Review & finish): 12 of 24
Still open on 2026-01-20: 12 of 24, stopped at:
Practice details: 1 of 24, open 5 days
Connect calendar: 7 of 24, open 4 to 41 days (median 16 days)
Invite your team: 3 of 24, open 6, 11 and 19 days
Review & finish: 1 of 24, open 2 days
Reached Review & finish: 13 of 24 (the 12 finished plus the 1 still open there)
Key Findings
[HIGH] (stall at Connect calendar) Connect calendar is where setups stop most: 7 of the 24 setups started (7 of the 12 still open) were open at that step on 2026-01-20, and they had sat there longest, 4 to 41 days (median 16). In the 12 finished setups, Connect calendar was also the step left open longest in 8 of 12.
[MEDIUM] (stall at Invite your team) Invite your team is the second most common stopping point: 3 of 24 setups started (3 of the 12 still open), open 6, 11 and 19 days.
[LOW] (other steps) 1 of 24 was open at Practice details (5 days) and 1 of 24 at Review & finish (2 days). No setup was open at Sign in, because a setup only counts as started once someone has signed in.
Representative Quotes
None — this session has no participants.
Recommendations
Run a moderated usability test of the setup flow with both Practice Administrators and IT Administrators, focused on Connect calendar and Invite your team, to find out why setups stop there.
Ask the dashboard owners whether the signed-in person's role can be shown per setup, so later reviews can tell Practice Administrator setups from IT Administrator ones.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Why do setups stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team? A dashboard can't show reasons: it records where a setup is open and for how long, not what the person at that step was thinking or waiting for.
Do stopped setups eventually finish, or are they abandoned? Re-check these 12 open setups at the next review.

sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

sources.title: Interview — IT Administrator on Schedule Access and Staff Invites
sources.excerpt:
Objective
In the 2026-02-03 usability test, 3 of 4 Practice Administrators stopped at Connect calendar because they did not think they could approve Compass AI's access to patient appointments, and both IT Administrators asked which fields are read before connecting ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:51-52 ). This session asked one IT Administrator who approves access requests across practices what has to happen before a new system can read a practice's appointment schedule, and who can start that. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training (in 2026-02-10-ambient-scribe-medication-flag-concept/session-notes.md:62 , "onboarding" means training copy for clinicians).
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is an IT Administrator who handles access requests for systems used across Meridian's practices. They had not used the Compass AI practice setup flow. The researcher described steps 3 (Connect calendar) and 4 (Invite your team) as the 2026-02-03 build shows them, and what the step 3 screen does and doesn't say, without sharing what other participants said. The participant did not name the scheduling system that holds the appointment schedule, and these notes don't record which system it is. This is their account of the approval process, not a review of its records.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (schedule access: privacy review) In their account, any new system that reads the appointment schedule needs a privacy review request before it is connected, and a Practice Administrator can't start one: requests are filed by IT. A practice that wants the calendar connected has to ask IT to file the request. They didn't know whether one had been filed for Compass AI.
[MEDIUM] (schedule access: still PHI) They described scheduling as the lowest-risk data on the CMIO's PHI ordering, but still PHI: the schedule carries patient names and, depending on the fields read, visit reasons. They saw this as consistent with the ordering, not a contradiction of it, because the ordering ranks the risk and doesn't remove the review.
Representative Quotes
"Lowest risk isn't no risk. It's still patient names on a schedule. It still goes through privacy review, it just shouldn't take long." — IT Administrator, P160
"A practice admin can't put in that request. They call us, we file it. If the screen just asks them to click connect, it's asking the wrong person." — IT Administrator, P160
Recommendations
On Connect calendar, route an administrator who can't approve schedule access to IT, consistent with the "Send to IT for approval" path recommended on 2026-02-03 ( 2026-02-03-usability-test-compass-ai-practice-setup-flow/session-notes.md:75-76 ).
Before more practices set up, confirm with IT whether a privacy review request for Compass AI reading the appointment schedule has been filed, and list the fields it covers.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Has a privacy review request for Compass AI's schedule access been filed, and which fields does it cover?
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through the setup flow's invites, or both? The participant didn't know.

questions.question: What is the current session timeout?

seeded.answer: The current session timeout is 10 minutes, and IT Security has confirmed it is not adjustable per feature [1][2]. The February 17, 2026 contextual inquiry found that during a session lock, the ambient-scribe widget freezes with no message, leading four out of five clinicians to assume their draft was lost and restart dictation [3]. One nurse practitioner reported experiencing locks “most afternoons, at least once” when stepping away from the workstation during a visit [2]. The SSO/MFA interview from May 20, 2025, also noted a potential conflict between security wanting a 15-minute timeout and clinical operations preferring 4 hours [4].

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

sources.title: Interview — IT Security on SSO/MFA Modernization Impact
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand planned SSO/MFA changes and their anticipated impact on clinical workflow before any AI feature is layered on top of authentication-dependent sessions.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 40 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (session timeout) Planned MFA rollout would introduce a shared-workstation re-authentication requirement every 15 minutes, down from the current 4 hours — flagged internally as likely to cause clinician pushback based on prior rollout feedback, independent of any AI feature.
[MEDIUM] (badge-tap workflow) Most units already use badge-tap proximity login for shared workstations; new MFA plan hasn't yet been confirmed to work with the existing badge-tap hardware.
[MEDIUM] (AI session risk) If an AI ambient scribe session is mid-recording when a forced re-auth occurs, current design has no defined behavior — could lose the in-progress draft.
Representative Quotes
"Security wants 15 minutes, clinical ops wants 4 hours, and nobody's told me yet who wins that argument, but I have to build for one of them." — IT Security Engineer, P31
"Nobody's asked what happens to an active AI recording session if the screen locks mid-visit. That's going to be a real incident the first time it happens." — IT Security Engineer, P31
Recommendations
Flag the ambient-scribe-mid-recording + forced-reauth interaction to the ambient scribe engineering team immediately as an unhandled edge case.
Push for a joint decision meeting between Security and Clinical Ops on the session timeout conflict before MFA rollout, independent of Compass AI.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm badge-tap hardware compatibility with new MFA plan.
Get the ambient scribe team's answer on session-loss behavior into a future usability test script.

sources.title: Interview — IT Security on SSO/MFA Modernization Impact
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand planned SSO/MFA changes and their anticipated impact on clinical workflow before any AI feature is layered on top of authentication-dependent sessions.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 40 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (session timeout) Planned MFA rollout would introduce a shared-workstation re-authentication requirement every 15 minutes, down from the current 4 hours — flagged internally as likely to cause clinician pushback based on prior rollout feedback, independent of any AI feature.
[MEDIUM] (badge-tap workflow) Most units already use badge-tap proximity login for shared workstations; new MFA plan hasn't yet been confirmed to work with the existing badge-tap hardware.
[MEDIUM] (AI session risk) If an AI ambient scribe session is mid-recording when a forced re-auth occurs, current design has no defined behavior — could lose the in-progress draft.
Representative Quotes
"Security wants 15 minutes, clinical ops wants 4 hours, and nobody's told me yet who wins that argument, but I have to build for one of them." — IT Security Engineer, P31
"Nobody's asked what happens to an active AI recording session if the screen locks mid-visit. That's going to be a real incident the first time it happens." — IT Security Engineer, P31
Recommendations
Flag the ambient-scribe-mid-recording + forced-reauth interaction to the ambient scribe engineering team immediately as an unhandled edge case.
Push for a joint decision meeting between Security and Clinical Ops on the session timeout conflict before MFA rollout, independent of Compass AI.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm badge-tap hardware compatibility with new MFA plan.
Get the ambient scribe team's answer on session-loss behavior into a future usability test script.

seeded.answer: The current session timeout is 10 minutes, and IT Security has confirmed this is not adjustable per feature [1][2]. The February 17, 2026 contextual inquiry found that during a session lock, the ambient-scribe widget freezes with no message, leading four out of five clinicians to assume their draft was lost and restart dictation [3]. One nurse practitioner reported experiencing locks “most afternoons, at least once” when stepping away from the workstation during a visit [2]. The SSO/MFA interview from May 20, 2025, also noted a potential conflict between security wanting a 15-minute timeout and clinical operations preferring 4 hours [4].

Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder

This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.

[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

sources.title: Ambient Scribe GA Candidate — First 4 Weeks Adoption Topline
sources.excerpt:
Covers the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout, per the 2026-01-27 dashboard review ( raw/2026-01-27-dashboard-review-ambient-scribe-ga-adoption/ ).
Clinicians shown confidence highlighting skim high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort — directionally consistent with the GA-candidate usability finding that visible uncertainty, not raw accuracy, changes reviewing behavior.
Adoption is uneven by role: attending physicians are opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments.

sources.title: Dashboard review — Ambient scribe GA candidate adoption
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Manually review the internal usage dashboard for the ambient scribe GA release candidate to see whether adoption and engagement patterns in real usage match what the GA-candidate usability round found — particularly whether the per-line confidence highlighting is actually changing reviewing behavior at scale, not just in the moderated session.
Method
Method: Manual dashboard review (no moderated session, no participants) — internal analytics dashboard covering the first 4 weeks of GA-candidate rollout
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: none — this is an analytics review, not a research session; see participants.md in this folder for why
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (trust) Clinicians who were shown confidence highlighting skim high-confidence lines at roughly double the rate of the pre-highlighting cohort — directionally consistent with the usability round's finding that visible uncertainty, not raw accuracy, changes reviewing behavior.
[LOW] (adoption) Adoption is uneven by role: attending physicians are opting in at a noticeably higher rate than residents in the same departments, worth understanding qualitatively rather than assuming it's a training gap.
Recommendations
Feed this dashboard pattern back into findings/ambient-scribe.md as corroborating evidence for the confidence-highlighting result, rather than treating it as a separate finding.
Consider a short follow-up interview round specifically on the physician/resident adoption gap.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Is the physician/resident adoption gap explained by workflow differences, trust, or something else entirely? Dashboard data alone can't answer this.

sources.title: Survey — Clinician Burnout & Documentation Burden Baseline
sources.participants: Participants: 287 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, Physician Assistant, Registered Nurse
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Establish a pre-AI-rollout baseline of self-reported burnout and documentation burden, so future surveys can measure whether Compass AI tools move the needle.
Method
Method: Anonymous org-wide survey, 15 questions (validated burnout subscale + custom documentation items)
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[HIGH] (documentation as burnout driver) Documentation burden ranked as the #1 self-selected contributor to burnout among physicians specifically (52%), ahead of patient volume (31%) and administrative meetings (12%).
[MEDIUM] (after-hours charting) 64% of physician respondents report regularly completing documentation after clinic hours ('pajama time'), averaging a self-reported 1.2 hours/day.
[MEDIUM] (baseline caution) Respondents were told this survey relates to a future AI initiative, which may have primed more favorable-than-baseline attitudes toward documentation-reducing tools — worth noting as a methodological caveat for anyone comparing to the February nursing survey, which didn't mention AI in its framing.
Representative Quotes
"I love this job. I do not love finishing my notes at 9pm after my kids are in bed. If AI fixes that, I'm in." — Physician, P84 (survey open-ended)
"Just don't let 'AI will fix documentation' become the excuse to skip fixing the actual EHR problems underneath it." — Nurse Practitioner, P91 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Use this survey as the official baseline metric for measuring Compass AI's impact on documentation burden and after-hours charting in future re-surveys (e.g., 6 and 12 months post-rollout).
Note the framing caveat explicitly in any report comparing this dataset to the February nursing survey.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Schedule a repeat of this exact survey instrument 6 months after ambient scribe GA rollout for comparison.

questions.question: How aware were staff of the Compass AI initiatives?

seeded.answer: According to a survey of 421 staff members, 71% of clinical staff reported awareness of Compass AI initiatives, while only 34% of non-clinical staff were aware [1]. This suggests internal communications have been clinically focused and may need broadening if non-clinical rollouts, such as scheduling, proceed [1]. One non-clinical staff member stated, “I hear about this AI stuff from clinical friends but nobody’s told admin staff what’s actually happening or if it affects us” [1].

sources.title: Survey — All-Staff AI Readiness Pulse Survey
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Take an org-wide temperature check on AI readiness/sentiment heading into 2026, as input to roadmap prioritization and communications planning.
Method
Method: Org-wide anonymous pulse survey, 10 questions
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[MEDIUM] (awareness gap) Only 34% of non-clinical staff reported being aware Compass AI initiatives were underway at all, versus 71% of clinical staff — suggesting internal communications have been clinically focused and may need broadening if non-clinical rollouts (e.g., scheduling) proceed.
[MEDIUM] (sentiment trend (directional, not causal)) Among clinical respondents, favorable sentiment toward AI-assisted documentation was somewhat higher than the March-ish baseline period, though this survey used different question wording than February's, so it's directional context rather than a clean comparison.
[LOW] (top requested feature) When asked what AI feature they'd most want next, 'appointment scheduling help' was the top write-in among non-clinical/admin staff, and 'documentation time savings' remained the top pick among clinical staff — consistent with priorities identified all year.
Representative Quotes
"I hear about this AI stuff from clinical friends but nobody's told admin staff what's actually happening or if it affects us." — Non-clinical/administrative staff, P112 (survey open-ended)
Recommendations
Broaden internal communications about Compass AI to non-clinical staff specifically before any admin-facing pilot (e.g., scheduling chatbot) goes live, given the awareness gap found here.
If a clean sentiment trend is wanted for 2026 reporting, re-run the exact February nursing survey instrument rather than a new pulse survey, to get a true apples-to-apples comparison.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Decide with leadership whether the September burnout survey or a repeat of the February survey is the better instrument for the planned 6-month post-GA comparison.

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.
