sources.title: Usability Test — Compass AI Practice Setup Flow
sources.participants: Participants: 6 — P154 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P155 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P156 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P157 — Practice Administrator (admin-staff) ×1, P158 — IT Administrator (it) ×1, P159 — IT Administrator (it) ×1
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-01-20 dashboard review found setups of Compass AI for a practice stopping most at Connect calendar (7 of 24 setups started) and then at Invite your team (3 of 24), and said a dashboard can't show why ( 2026-01-20-dashboard-review-compass-ai-practice-setup-completion/session-notes.md:45-46,72 ). This session watched administrators go through the practice setup flow to find out what happens at those two steps. It is about admin setup of Compass AI, not staff training.
Method
Method: Moderated usability test, remote, think-aloud, 60 min/session, one participant per session
Researcher: Priya Patel (moderator)
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Participants: 6 — 4 Practice Administrators (P154-P157) and 2 IT Administrators (P158, P159)
Steps tested, in order: 1 Sign in with Meridian SSO; 2 Practice details; 3 Connect calendar (read access to the practice's appointment schedule); 4 Invite your team (gives clinicians and staff access to Compass AI and sends them an email); 5 Review & finish.
Build: Steps 3 and 4 are required in this build. There is no "Connect later" and no "Skip for now"; the only way past each step is to complete it.
Design context: At session setup, the designer, Sam Okafor, stated that the calendar step is required because the scribe attaches recordings to scheduled encounters.
Test environment: Participants signed in with their own Meridian SSO and were asked to set up as they would for their own practice. The environment was a test one: step 3 connected to a prepared sandbox calendar standing in for the practice's schedule, and step 4 used a prepared test staff list, so no real schedule was read and no real staff were emailed.
Test accommodation: When a participant stopped at step 3, the moderator told them it was the sandbox calendar and let them continue. Every participant completed step 3 this way or on their own, so completing step 3 in this session is not a result.
Not covered: The step 4 screen doesn't say when the invite email is sent, and these notes don't record when this build sends it. How Compass AI access is provisioned (through SSO groups or through these invites) wasn't known to the moderator and isn't recorded in the corpus.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (calendar: who can approve) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P155, P157) stopped at Connect calendar and wouldn't connect it: it gives Compass AI access to patient appointments, and they did not think they could approve that. Each said it was IT's decision. The fourth (P156) asked the moderator whether connecting the schedule was theirs to approve before going on. All 4 continued only on the sandbox calendar (see Test accommodation).
[MEDIUM] (calendar: what is read) Both IT Administrators (P158, P159) connected the calendar, but only after asking which fields are read (for example, whether visit reasons are included). The screen doesn't list them; the moderator couldn't answer, and both went on without an answer.
[HIGH] (invite: timing and training) 3 of 4 Practice Administrators (P154, P156, P157) hesitated at Invite your team. They weren't sure whether the email goes out when they finish the step or at Review & finish, and they didn't want staff emailed before champion training is booked for the practice. P155 entered the test staff list and went on without comment.
[MEDIUM] (invite: provisioning) One IT Administrator (P159) asked whether the invites create accounts or rely on the SSO groups staff are already in. The moderator couldn't answer, and the corpus doesn't record how access is provisioned.
[LOW] (sign in and practice details) No issues at Sign in or Practice details: 6 of 6 participants completed both without help or comment on a problem.
Representative Quotes
"That's patient names and visit reasons. That's not my call — that's IT's." — Practice Administrator, P154
"Is this mine to say yes to? I'd normally send anything like this to IT." — Practice Administrator, P156
"If forty people get an email before anyone's booked training, my phone rings all afternoon." — Practice Administrator, P157
"Before I connect it I want to know what it pulls. Times and providers, fine. Visit reasons, that's a different conversation." — IT Administrator, P158
"Does this make them an account, or does it just use the groups they're already in? Because if it's a separate list, I'm the one keeping it in sync." — IT Administrator, P159
Recommendations
List the fields read from the appointment schedule on the Connect calendar step.
Add a "Send to IT for approval" path on Connect calendar for an administrator who can't approve the access themselves.
Say on the Invite your team screen when the invite email is sent.
Let administrators schedule the invite email for a date, so it can go out once training is booked.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How is Compass AI access provisioned: through SSO groups, through these invites, or both? Ask the setup flow's engineering team.
When does this build send the invite email: at step 4 or at Review & finish?
Check the setup dashboard after any copy change to these steps, to see whether setups still stop at Connect calendar and Invite your team.

questions.question: What haven't we learned yet about care coordinators?

seeded.answer:
The sources indicate several things remain unknown about care coordinators. Firstly, it hasn’t been measured how often coordinators follow a ranked order without their own judgement [1][2][3]. Real-world triage speed also remains unmeasured, though a simulated test showed a faster time with AI ranking (6.5 minutes) compared to a chronological queue (9 minutes) [4].

Additionally, the sources don’t show how many alerts are repeats for the same patient [3], or how often the after-visit summary misses changes [1]. It’s also unclear whether the 2025 ranking was accurate or what it was based on [1][3][4], and whether the idea of capturing override reasons reached the data science team [2][1][3]. Finally, it is not known how accurate the 2025 ranking was, and what it was based on [5][1][3][4].

sources.title: Care Coordination & Alert Triage
sources.excerpt: Still open after the 2026 interviews: how often the after-visit summary misses changes; whether the 2025 queue showed coordinators what its ranking was based on; how accurate the ranking is; real-world triage speed; how often coordinators follow a ranked order without judgement (no measurement of rubber-stamping); and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team.

sources.title: Interview — Care Coordinator Supervisor on Queue Oversight
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Get a care coordinator supervisor's view of what oversight they would need if alerts were AI-ranked, following up the August 2025 supervisor's concern that speed gains could mask rubber-stamping, and the override-reason capture designed after that test. The participant is a different person from P79, the supervisor in the August 2025 test.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant leads an ambulatory care coordination team. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built, and the override-reason capture wireflow is designed and in review, not built. They had not seen the August 2025 screens before; they reacted to a description of the ranked queue and the override-reason flow in this session. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (oversight) If alerts were AI-ranked, they would want a record of the order each coordinator was shown and what the coordinator did with each alert, so they could look back at a case when something went wrong. They would also use override reasons for coaching, to see how a coordinator is judging risk, not only for model tuning. That raises a question the current design doesn't settle: the wireflow logs reasons for model-tuning review and says they are "not surfaced to other coordinators", but doesn't say whether supervisors see them.
[MEDIUM] (alert volume) They estimated that heavy days run "maybe 30 to 60 alerts" per coordinator, and that many of them are administrative rather than clinical. This is their informal estimate; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (rubber-stamping) They shared the August 2025 supervisor's worry that a ranked order could be followed without judgement, but said they'd only know if it was happening by looking at what coordinators did with the order. This is a perspective, not a measurement; nothing about how often coordinators follow a ranking has been measured.
Representative Quotes
"If something goes wrong, I need to see what order they were shown and what they did with it. Otherwise I'm coaching blind." — Care Coordinator Supervisor, P132
"The reasons are the useful part for me. They tell me how someone's thinking about risk." — Care Coordinator Supervisor, P132
Recommendations
Decide who can see override reasons (model-tuning review only, or supervisors as well) before the reason-capture wireflow leaves review, and say so in the design.
If a ranked queue is piloted, record the order shown and each coordinator's action, so rubber-stamping can be looked for in data rather than assumed.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without judgement is not measured, and can't be until something is built and logged.
Real alert volumes per coordinator are not known; the 30 to 60 figure is one supervisor's estimate.
Whether the override-capture idea was shared with the Data Science team working on the care-gap flagging model, as the August 2025 session suggested, isn't recorded.

sources.title: Interview — Complex Care Coordinator on Alert Volume
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand where alert noise comes from for a coordinator on a high-risk panel, and whether AI ranking addresses it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the May 2026 supervisor's estimate that many alerts are administrative rather than clinical.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on a complex care team with a high-risk panel. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (repeat alerts) For them, the main source of noise is repeat alerts for the same patient, more than the order the alerts come in. They would want alerts grouped by patient before any ranking is applied, so that they deal with one patient once rather than meeting them several times down the queue. This is their account; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (patient history) Their judgement of a patient's risk leans on knowing that patient's history, which a ranking based on the alert alone wouldn't have. This is a second voice alongside P81's 2025 comment about knowing a patient's history, from a different coordinator on a different kind of panel.
Representative Quotes
"It's not the order that gets me, it's seeing the same patient four times. Put them together first, then rank them if you want." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
"I know these patients. Half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
Recommendations
Explore grouping alerts by patient as a step before ranking, and test it with coordinators on high-risk panels.
Keep patient history in view when ranking signals are next revisited, in line with the August 2025 recommendation.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How many alerts are repeats for the same patient is not measured; this is one coordinator's account.
How the 2025 ranking was built and how accurate it is are still not documented, and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team isn't recorded.
Real-world triage speed and how often coordinators would follow a ranked order without judgement are not measured.

sources.title: Care Coordinators' Mental Model of Alert Ranking
sources.excerpt: The designer's paraphrase of the coordinator view: the system should defer to the coordinator's sense of a patient's history-driven risk — an experience-weighted judgment call. In 2025 this rested on one coordinator, P81: "I wanted to tell it 'no, this one's more urgent because I know this patient's history,' but there was nowhere to put that." It now rests on two team coordinators. In 2026, P81 said their most common reason for moving an alert is something the patient or a family member said on the phone that isn't in the chart yet, and P134, on a complex care team with a high-risk panel, said "half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter" (both observed: what they said, not measured). Participants saw the ranking weight recency more heavily than their own sense of clinical risk; 4 of 5 disagreed with the AI's top-3 ranking on at least one of three test queues. There's no way for a coordinator's override to feed back into the ranking. Triage of a 20-item queue was still faster with the AI ranking than with a chronological queue in this simulated test (avg 6.5 min vs. 9 min).

sources.title: Interview — New Care Coordinator on Learning the Queue
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how a care coordinator who is new to the role learns the team's working conventions, and what an AI-ranked alert queue would mean for someone who doesn't yet have the experience to judge it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the undocumented colour-coding first described in the January 2025 baseline.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory team who has been in the role for under a year. They read the signed visit notes clinicians produce, including scribe-drafted ones, but don't use the scribe themselves. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (learning by shadowing) They learned the team's conventions, including what the shared spreadsheet's colours mean and which alerts can safely wait, by shadowing experienced coordinators, with nothing written down to check against later. They thought a ranked queue might help newer coordinators most, because it would stand in for the judgement they haven't built yet. But they said newer coordinators would also be the least able to tell when the ranking is wrong. This is their own reflection; nothing was observed or measured in this session.
[MEDIUM] (chart review time) In their first months, chart review before an outreach call took them "closer to 20 minutes at first", which is longer than the 8-14 minutes the January 2025 baseline described for experienced coordinators. They said it has come down since. This is an informal recollection, not a timed measurement.
Representative Quotes
"Nobody gave me a list. I sat next to people for two weeks and picked up what the colours meant and which alerts could wait." — Care Coordinator, P135
"A ranked list would've been great my first month. But I wouldn't have known if it was wrong, and that's the scary part." — Care Coordinator, P135
Recommendations
Treat newer coordinators as a distinct group when the ranked queue is next tested: check whether they can spot a wrong ranking, not just whether they work faster with one.
Write down the team conventions that are currently passed on by shadowing (colour meanings, which alerts can wait), so that any design that carries or replaces them has a source to work from.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
How long chart review takes for coordinators in their first year is not measured; "closer to 20 minutes at first" is one coordinator's recollection.
How accurate the 2025 ranking is, and what it was based on, are still not documented, so it isn't known how often a newer coordinator would meet a wrong ranking.
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without their own judgement has not been measured, for newer coordinators or anyone else.

Objective
Understand where alert noise comes from for a coordinator on a high-risk panel, and whether AI ranking addresses it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the May 2026 supervisor's estimate that many alerts are administrative rather than clinical.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on a complex care team with a high-risk panel. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (repeat alerts) For them, the main source of noise is repeat alerts for the same patient, more than the order the alerts come in. They would want alerts grouped by patient before any ranking is applied, so that they deal with one patient once rather than meeting them several times down the queue. This is their account; no queue data was reviewed in this session.
[MEDIUM] (patient history) Their judgement of a patient's risk leans on knowing that patient's history, which a ranking based on the alert alone wouldn't have. This is a second voice alongside P81's 2025 comment about knowing a patient's history, from a different coordinator on a different kind of panel.
Representative Quotes
"It's not the order that gets me, it's seeing the same patient four times. Put them together first, then rank them if you want." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
"I know these patients. Half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter." — Care Coordinator (complex care), P134
Recommendations
Explore grouping alerts by patient as a step before ranking, and test it with coordinators on high-risk panels.
Keep patient history in view when ranking signals are next revisited, in line with the August 2025 recommendation.

How many alerts are repeats for the same patient is not measured; this is one coordinator's account.
How the 2025 ranking was built and how accurate it is are still not documented, and whether the override-capture idea reached the data-science team isn't recorded.
Real-world triage speed and how often coordinators would follow a ranked order without judgement are not measured.

sources.title: Care Coordinators' Mental Model of Alert Ranking
sources.excerpt: The designer's paraphrase of the coordinator view: the system should defer to the coordinator's sense of a patient's history-driven risk — an experience-weighted judgment call. In 2025 this rested on one coordinator, P81: "I wanted to tell it 'no, this one's more urgent because I know this patient's history,' but there was nowhere to put that." It now rests on two team coordinators. In 2026, P81 said their most common reason for moving an alert is something the patient or a family member said on the phone that isn't in the chart yet, and P134, on a complex care team with a high-risk panel, said "half of deciding who's at risk is knowing what happened to them last winter" (both observed: what they said, not measured). Participants saw the ranking weight recency more heavily than their own sense of clinical risk; 4 of 5 disagreed with the AI's top-3 ranking on at least one of three test queues. There's no way for a coordinator's override to feed back into the ranking. Triage of a 20-item queue was still faster with the AI ranking than with a chronological queue in this simulated test (avg 6.5 min vs. 9 min).

sources.title: Interview — New Care Coordinator on Learning the Queue
sources.excerpt:
Objective
Understand how a care coordinator who is new to the role learns the team's working conventions, and what an AI-ranked alert queue would mean for someone who doesn't yet have the experience to judge it, following up the August 2025 alert-triage test and the undocumented colour-coding first described in the January 2025 baseline.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a care coordinator on an ambulatory team who has been in the role for under a year. They read the signed visit notes clinicians produce, including scribe-drafted ones, but don't use the scribe themselves. Their team works the chronological queue; the AI-ranked queue hasn't been built. They reacted to a description of the ranked queue, not to screens. They did not take part in any earlier session.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (learning by shadowing) They learned the team's conventions, including what the shared spreadsheet's colours mean and which alerts can safely wait, by shadowing experienced coordinators, with nothing written down to check against later. They thought a ranked queue might help newer coordinators most, because it would stand in for the judgement they haven't built yet. But they said newer coordinators would also be the least able to tell when the ranking is wrong. This is their own reflection; nothing was observed or measured in this session.
[MEDIUM] (chart review time) In their first months, chart review before an outreach call took them "closer to 20 minutes at first", which is longer than the 8-14 minutes the January 2025 baseline described for experienced coordinators. They said it has come down since. This is an informal recollection, not a timed measurement.

"Nobody gave me a list. I sat next to people for two weeks and picked up what the colours meant and which alerts could wait." — Care Coordinator, P135
"A ranked list would've been great my first month. But I wouldn't have known if it was wrong, and that's the scary part." — Care Coordinator, P135

Treat newer coordinators as a distinct group when the ranked queue is next tested: check whether they can spot a wrong ranking, not just whether they work faster with one.
Write down the team conventions that are currently passed on by shadowing (colour meanings, which alerts can wait), so that any design that carries or replaces them has a source to work from.

How long chart review takes for coordinators in their first year is not measured; "closer to 20 minutes at first" is one coordinator's recollection.
How accurate the 2025 ranking is, and what it was based on, are still not documented, so it isn't known how often a newer coordinator would meet a wrong ranking.
How often coordinators would follow a ranked order without their own judgement has not been measured, for newer coordinators or anyone else.

questions.question: What is unresolved about the session timeout?

seeded.answer:
The interaction between the session lock and an in-progress Ambient Scribe recording is unresolved [1]. Specifically, the locked state currently reads as silent data loss, causing clinicians to assume their draft is lost and restart dictation, despite the draft being preserved server-side; 4 of 5 clinicians shadowed exhibited this behavior [1][2].

While IT Security has confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout policy is fixed and cannot be adjusted per feature [3][1][4], a UI-only fix to display an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is technically feasible [1][2]. The team is currently designing a recovery flow to address this, focusing on UI messaging rather than changing the timeout policy itself [4]. Further work is needed to determine how this paused state should behave in shared exam-room workstations [5].

sources.title: Ambient Scribe — Post-GA Refinements
sources.excerpt: Session lock during active dictation currently reads as silent data loss, even though it isn't. The locked state's interaction with an in-progress recording was flagged as unresolved in encounter-view 's own notes, sourced from a May 2025 SSO/MFA interview side comment. Direct observation confirms the practical impact: all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed a locked session had destroyed their draft and restarted dictation from scratch, even though the draft is preserved server-side. IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle-timeout policy itself is fixed, but an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is a UI-only fix, not a policy change.

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.

seeded.answer:
The interaction between the session lock and an in-progress Ambient Scribe recording is unresolved [1]. Specifically, the locked state currently reads as silent data loss, causing all 4 of 5 shadowed clinicians to assume their draft was lost and restart dictation, despite the draft being preserved server-side [1][2].

While IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout policy is fixed and cannot be adjusted per feature [3][4], a UI-only fix to display an explicit "paused, draft preserved" state is technically feasible [3][1]. The team is designing a flow to replace the silent freeze with this explicit state, covering the interaction from the idle timeout firing through resumed dictation [4]. However, how this paused state will behave on shared exam-room workstations—when another clinician signs in during a lock—remains unaddressed [5]. Additionally, it’s unclear if the paused state will change clinician behavior or just their understanding, and re-testing is planned after implementation [1][5].

sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.

"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder

Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

sources.title: Contextual Inquiry — Session Lock During Active Ambient Scribe Dictation
sources.participants: Participants: 5 — Physician, Nurse Practitioner, IT Security
sources.excerpt:
Objective
encounter-view.md 's component notes flag the locked state's interaction with an in-progress ambient scribe recording as an open edge case, raised as a side note in the 2025-05-20 SSO/MFA interview but never directly studied. This session shadows clinicians through their normal SSO/MFA idle-timeout window while actively dictating, to observe what actually happens today and what they expect/want instead.
Method
Method: Contextual inquiry / shadowing, 5 clinicians observed through at least one natural idle-timeout event during a real or simulated dictation session, plus 1 IT Security stakeholder interviewed on the technical constraints
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Key Findings
[CRITICAL] (silent draft loss) In the current build, a session lock mid-recording simply freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message; 4 of 5 clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started re-dictating from scratch after re-authenticating, even though the draft is server-side and actually survives the lock.
[HIGH] (no explicit paused state) There is no visual distinction between "recording," "frozen because locked," and "actually stopped" — participants could not tell which state they were in without asking a shadowing observer.
[MEDIUM] (re-auth friction stacks) Clinicians already re-authenticate frequently for unrelated reasons (badge-tap SSO renewals); a lock during dictation is perceived as "one more annoying re-login," not as a distinct, expected safety behavior — this framing gap likely drives the abandon-and-redictate behavior above as much as the missing UI does.
[LOW] (IT Security confirms feasibility) IT Security confirmed the 10-minute idle timeout is not adjustable per-feature, but confirmed an explicit "paused, draft preserved" UI state is technically straightforward to add without changing the timeout policy itself.
Representative Quotes
"I genuinely thought I'd lost it. I've just gotten used to starting over when the screen locks, so I didn't even try to check." — Physician, Family Medicine, P31
"If it said 'paused, nothing lost, just log back in,' I'd believe it and wait. Right now it just looks broken." — Nurse Practitioner, P33
"The timeout window itself is a hard policy constraint, but what the screen tells the clinician during that window is entirely a product decision — that part isn't locked down." — IT Security stakeholder
Recommendations
Add an explicit "paused — draft preserved, re-authenticate to resume" state to the encounter-view / ambient-scribe-widget lock interaction, replacing the current silent freeze.
Do not attempt to change or extend the idle-timeout policy itself — per IT Security, treat it as fixed and solve this entirely at the UI-messaging layer.
Pair the new state with brief messaging that reframes the lock as an expected safety behavior rather than an unrelated login interruption, to counter the "one more annoying re-login" framing found here.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
Confirm with IT Security whether the same "paused, preserved" messaging pattern should extend to other session-timeout-adjacent surfaces beyond ambient scribe.
Re-test the abandon-and-redictate behavior once the explicit paused state ships, to confirm it actually changes clinician behavior and not just their stated understanding.

sources.title: Interview — Nurse Practitioner on Session Lock and Shared Exam-Room Workstations
sources.excerpt:
Objective
The 2026-02-17 contextual inquiry found that a session lock during active dictation freezes the ambient-scribe widget with no message, and that all 4 shadowed clinicians assumed the draft was lost and started dictating again, although the draft survives server-side (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:38-41, read with correction-2026-09-27.md in that folder). A recovery flow with an explicit paused, draft-preserved state is designed but has not shipped. That session did not look at exam-room workstations shared by several clinicians. This session asked a primary care nurse practitioner, two months later, what a lock looks like in their visits and how a shared workstation affects it.
Method
Method: 1:1 interview, 45 min
Researcher: Priya Patel
Full participant roster: see participants.md in this folder
Context: The participant is a nurse practitioner in an ambulatory primary care clinic, about five years in that role. They use the ambient scribe for most visits. Exam rooms in their clinic have a workstation that clinicians share across the day, signing in with a badge tap. The idle timeout is 10 minutes and is not adjustable per feature (2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:49-50). The paused state has not shipped, so a lock still freezes the widget with no message. They did not take part in any earlier session, including the 2026-02-17 inquiry. This is an interview about their own practice; nothing was shown or observed.
Key Findings
[HIGH] (lock during a visit) A lock happens to them when they step away from the workstation to the exam table within the room, typically for the physical exam, and the idle timeout fires while the scribe is listening. When they come back the widget looks frozen and shows no message. Their practice is to re-authenticate and scroll through the draft to see what is still there before they say anything more. They described learning this after re-dictating a visit summary early on and then finding the original draft intact; that is their account of their own practice, not an observed change. They put locks at "most afternoons, at least once", an informal impression.
[HIGH] (shared workstations) Two or more clinicians use the same exam-room workstation on a clinic day, each signing in with a badge tap. They do not know what happens to their in-progress draft if a colleague signs in on that workstation while their session is locked, and they did not want to find out with a patient's visit. So they stop the scribe before leaving a room, even mid-visit, and start it again when they return. That avoids the question but splits one visit across several recordings, which they then have to read as one draft. How the product behaves in that case is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
[MEDIUM] (framing) They described the lock as one more sign-in in a day full of them, not as a safety behavior. That matches the framing the 2026-02-17 inquiry recorded ("one more annoying re-login", 2026-02-17-session-lock-during-dictation/session-notes.md:45-48); it is this participant's own description, and the earlier finding was not put to them.
[MEDIUM] (what would help) Asked what they would want to see after a lock, without being shown anything, they said a message that the draft is saved and whose session it belongs to. That is an expectation; the paused state has not shipped and was not shown.
Representative Quotes
"I come back from the exam table and it's just sitting there. No message. I badge back in and scroll through before I say another word." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
"Two of us use that room. I don't know what happens to my recording if someone else taps in, so I stop it before I walk out." — Nurse Practitioner (primary care), P148
Recommendations
Add the shared exam-room workstation to the review of the paused-state recovery flow: what a clinician sees after a lock when a colleague has signed in on the same workstation.
Make sure the paused-state message says whose draft is preserved, not only that a draft is.
When the paused state ships, re-test whether clinicians still stop the scribe before leaving a shared room, as well as whether they still re-dictate.
Follow-ups / Open Questions
What happens to an in-progress draft when another clinician signs in on the same workstation during a lock is not recorded in the corpus and was not settled here.
How often locks interrupt a visit is not measured; "most afternoons, at least once" is one nurse practitioner's impression.
Whether other clinicians stop the scribe before leaving a shared room is not known; this is one interview.
Whether the paused state changes behavior can only be tested once it ships, as the 2026-02-17 inquiry already noted.
